pivots are inserted, and thus the snail-screw, turned by men treading upon it, creates its rotations. Its elevation should be arranged at such an inclination that it corresponds to the description of a Pythagorean right-angled triangle <note>original: "pythagoricum trigonum orthogonium"</note>. That is, the length is divided into five parts, and the head of the screw is raised by three of those parts; thus the space from the perpendicular line to the lower openings <note>original: "imas nares"</note> will be four parts. The manner in which this should be done is illustrated at the end of the book.

<margin>
a. The snail-screw <term>coclea</term> <gloss>an Archimedean screw for lifting water</gloss> erected according to the ratio of the Pythagorean triangle.
b. The beams in which the screw turns.
</margin>

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts an Archimedean screw used for irrigation or drainage. The device consists of a wooden shaft with an internal spiral encased in a cylinder, tilted at an angle. The lower end is submerged in water, and the upper end is supported by a tall wooden pillar labeled 'b'. A large treadwheel labeled 'd' is attached to the center of the shaft, allowing humans to turn the device by treading on its rungs. Water is shown being lifted through the screw and discharging from the top into a wooden trough or basin. The letter 'a' labels the main body of the screw.</note>

Regarding the materials from which machines for drawing water <note>original: "organa ad hauriendam aquam"</note> are made, the methods by which they are completed, and the things that receive motion to provide rotations for infinite uses,

<summary>Vitruvius explains the proper angle of elevation for an Archimedean screw using the Pythagorean 3-4-5 triangle ratio and describes its operation via human power.</summary>
<keywords>Archimedean screw, Pythagorean triangle, hydraulics, water lifting, irrigation, mechanics, Vitruvius</keywords>
